title: Polycrisis Resilience Pathways
subtitle: Strategic Pathways for Reducing Human and Systemic Vulnerability in the 21st Century
description: Turns the polycrisis diagnosis into eight development pathways, scores their resilience co-benefits, and adds a prototype vulnerability index and a three-phase route to 2050.
contribution: Moves Polycrisis Resilience from diagnosis to programme: eight pathways, a co-benefit matrix, a nine-indicator prototype index for five regions, and a pace-based route to 2050, all built on World Bank data.

subjects.name: Pollution and contamination not elsewhere classified
Human impacts of climate change and human adaptation

abstract: Climate hazards, polluted air, water and food stress, poverty, conflict and weak institutions now act on the same people at the same time. This report turns that diagnosis into a programme. It sets out eight development pathways that lower human and systemic vulnerability, shows with World Bank data where each gap is widest, and scores which pathways deliver the most resilience co-benefits. It also proposes a prototype index and a three-phase route to 2050.

The eight pathways are economic convergence, clean energy, technology diffusion, climate adaptation, pollution reduction, water, food and resource security, human development, and infrastructure with institutions. The evidence comes from World Bank indicators for more than 180 countries, and the report labels each exhibit as published evidence, processed data, author judgement or an illustrative model. The index, the co-benefit scores and the modelled paths are prototypes, and the report presents its claim as integration and application rather than the founding of new fields.
coreProposition: Polycrisis Resilience can be strengthened through coordinated development pathways that reduce underlying human and systemic vulnerabilities while improving the capacity of societies to anticipate, absorb, adapt to and recover from interconnected disruptions. Development is a resilience strategy, sustainable convergence is essential, and transformation must be coordinated.

keyFindings.title: Development gaps are vulnerability gaps.
keyFindings.text: Across 188 countries, income per person explains about 73% of the variation in under-five mortality on a log scale, and each doubling of income goes with a rate about 43% lower. The report stresses that this is an association, not proof of cause.

keyFindings.title: Convergence is strong in the middle and absent at the bottom.
keyFindings.text: From 1990 to 2024 GDP per person rose 322% in upper-middle-income countries, 169% in lower-middle-income countries and 18% in low-income countries, which now sit at 1.7% of the high-income level. Electricity use in low-income countries (190 kWh a person) is where it stood in 1990.

keyFindings.title: Access gaps close slowest where they matter most.
keyFindings.text: At the 2010–2024 pace, low-income countries need about 380 years for universal clean cooking, 120 for safe water and 32 for electricity. Universal access by 2050 would need 15 times the current pace for cooking and 4.7 times for water. The report calls this a pace comparison, not a forecast.

keyFindings.title: Pollution does not fall on its own with growth.
keyFindings.text: PM2.5 exposure in 2023 was 49.6 µg/m³ in lower-middle-income countries, 31.3 in low-income and 13.0 in high-income countries, and 94% of countries exceed the WHO guideline.

keyFindings.title: Three pathways lead on co-benefits.
keyFindings.text: In an author-scored matrix (eight pathways against seven vulnerability components, 21 points), infrastructure and institutions score 16, economic convergence and clean energy 15 each, and pollution reduction 11. Scores within two points are treated as ties.

keyFindings.title: A prototype index orders five regions.
keyFindings.text: Built from nine indicators in seven components, the index runs from 24 in Sub-Saharan Africa to 91 in high-income economies (South Asia 51, Southeast Asia 63, Latin America and the Caribbean 73). The order holds in all ten weighting variants tested.

keyFindings.title: The binding constraint differs by region.
keyFindings.text: The weakest indicator is water and income in Sub-Saharan Africa, air quality in South Asia, water and governance in Southeast Asia and governance in Latin America, so pathways must be sequenced locally.

keyFindings.title: Five loops compound in both directions.
keyFindings.text: Energy and industrialization, climate and food, pollution and health, education and technology, and infrastructure and institutions can each run as a virtuous or vicious cycle. Across 142 countries electricity use and income move together (squared correlation 0.84 on logs).

keyFindings.title: Cost of capital is a resilience variable.
keyFindings.text: The same solar farm costs 82% more at a 15% cost of capital than at 6%, so lowering financing costs is one of the report's five practical priorities, with clearing the binding constraint first, counting every return, funding maintenance and publishing a repeated baseline.

bottomLine: A restrained, data-led framework whose own prototypes are clearly labelled. The index and co-benefit scores are the author's judgement on public data, not a validated model, and the report says the next step is to back-test them.

glossary.definition: The capacity of people, institutions, economies and the systems that connect them to anticipate, absorb, adapt to and recover from interconnected disruptions, while reducing the underlying human and systemic vulnerabilities that make those disruptions harmful.

Eight development-oriented pathways that act on interconnected risks to reduce human and systemic vulnerability: economic convergence, clean energy, technology diffusion, climate adaptation, pollution reduction, water, food and resource security, human development, and infrastructure with institutions.
The idea that an investment is valuable for all the vulnerabilities it removes together, not only the one it targets.
The closing of gaps in income, energy, services and technology between poorer and richer economies on a path that does not raise exposure to the hazards it is meant to reduce.
The weakest indicator or component of vulnerability in a place, which determines which pathway should come first.
The report's author-judged scoring of eight pathways against seven vulnerability components on a 0 to 3 scale, summed to a total out of 21.
A 0 to 100 index built from nine World Bank indicators in seven components, scored against the 5th and 95th percentile of countries and averaged with equal weights.
The difference between the 2010–2024 rate of progress on access to a service and the rate needed to reach universal access by 2050, treated as arithmetic rather than a forecast.
Stress in one system propagating to others until several fail together, the worst case of a polycrisis (Homer-Dixon and colleagues).
